query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating Cr into an AlCoFeNi high‐entropy alloy – for example, modifying it to an AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi composition – will increase the coercive field by promoting a hierarchical phase separation (a B2 matrix with embedded A2 precipitates) that nucleates magnetic vortices and enhances domain‐wall pinning.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoFeNi high‐entropy alloy with a more homogeneous or less hierarchically separated structure.
generation.intervention: Partially substitute one of the traditional magnetic elements (e.g., Co) with Cr during alloy synthesis to yield AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi.
generation.conditions: The alloys should be synthesized and annealed under identical processing conditions (e.g., same melting, cooling, and post‐annealing protocols) and characterized at room temperature under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically decomposed microstructure featuring an ordered, weakly ferromagnetic B2 matrix interspersed with disordered, strongly magnetic A2 precipitates that develop magnetic vortex states.
generation.mechanism: The introduction of Cr is expected to alter the exchange interactions so as to drive phase separation into B2 and A2 phases. The resulting nanoscale magnetic heterogeneity and the formation of vortices in the A2 regions provide additional pinning sites that retard magnetization reversal, thereby increasing the measured coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline homogeneous AlCoFeNi alloy, the Cr-containing variant (AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi) will show an increased coercive field when measured by magnetic hysteresis methods.
generation.baseline: AlCoFeNi high‐entropy alloy synthesized under the same processing conditions without Cr addition.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected only for alloys that have a propensity toward hierarchical phase separation. If processing conditions or compositions suppress phase separation, the coercivity enhancement may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative increase in coercivity is supported by the concept of vortex pinning in a heterogeneous magnetic microstructure, the precise magnitude of the increase is uncertain due to complex phase transformation kinetics and magnetic interactions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of high‐entropy alloys: one with the baseline AlCoFeNi composition and another with the modified AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi composition. Process both under identical conditions. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or X‐ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize the microstructure for evidence of hierarchical phase separation. Use a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) to obtain hysteresis loops and determine the coercive fields at room temperature.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (phase identification, size and distribution of phases)
Magnetic hysteresis loops to quantitatively extract the coercive field (Hc)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in coercive field compared to the baseline—or if the predicted hierarchical phase separation with magnetic vortex formation cannot be confirmed by microstructural analyses—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Highly complex magnetic behavior resulting from hierarchical phase separation in AlCo(Cr)FeNi high-entropy alloys

Abstract: SummaryMagnetic high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new category of high-performance magnetic materials, with multicomponent concentrated compositions and complex multi-phase structures. Although there have been numerous reports of their interesting magnetic properties, there is very limited understanding about the interplay between their hierarchical multi-phase structures and the resulting magnetic behavior. We reveal for the first time the influence of a hierarchically decomposed B2 + A2 structure in an AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA on the formation of magnetic vortex states within individual A2 (disordered BCC) precipitates, which are distributed in an ordered B2 matrix that is weakly ferromagnetic. Non-magnetic or weakly ferromagnetic B2 precipitates in large magnetic domains of the A2 phase, and strongly magnetic Fe-Co-rich interphase A2 regions, are also observed. These results provide important insight into the origin of coercivity in this HEA, which can be attributed to a complex magnetization process that includes the successive reversal of magnetic vortices.
